directions.name: Rule Observatory
directions.short: Observe rules across systems and through time.
directions.description: Trace the creation, reuse, revision, and retirement of rules in legal codes, judicial opinions, and organizational regulations. Connecting these records makes it possible to compare how different systems preserve and revise their rules.
directions.method: Longitudinal corpora · Citation networks · Text reuse
directions.question: How can we observe rules changing over time?

directions.name: Rule Dynamics
directions.description: Study how functional diversity, specialization, and coordination costs change with system size. Compare biological and social systems to ask which patterns recur and which depend on institutional context.
directions.method: Scaling analysis · Generative models · Cross-system comparison
directions.question: How does regulation change as systems grow?

directions.name: Theory-Based Prediction
directions.short: Understand persistence, change, and institutional memory.
directions.description: Ask how past citations, reused language, and network structure relate to future rule use and revision. Test what historical evidence can tell us about institutional inertia, adaptation, and the limits of prediction.
directions.method: Temporal networks · Survival analysis · Time-based evaluation
directions.question: What makes rules persist, change, or disappear?

directions.name: Rule Evolution Simulation
directions.short: Study AI, feedback, and institutional learning.
directions.description: Investigate how faster rule production interacts with human review, model diversity, and feedback. Develop experiments to ask when AI supports error correction and when correlated mistakes or delayed scrutiny undermine it.
directions.method: Agent-based models · AI intervention scenarios · Feedback experiments
directions.question: How might AI change institutional learning?

hypotheses.name: Partial self-evolution
hypotheses.question: Do rules have dynamics of their own?
hypotheses.text: Rule lineages, citation structures, reused language, and semantic positions may predict subsequent citation, revision, and disappearance even after considering human intentions and external conditions, indicating dynamics beyond individual institutional actors.

hypotheses.name: Critical transitions
hypotheses.question: When does a system lose its ability to recover?
hypotheses.text: Rule systems may have multiple stable states and undergo threshold transitions. Reduced diversity, concentrated citations, and delayed feedback may weaken resilience, with slower recovery, rising autocorrelation, and variability signaling transitions.

hypotheses.name: AI timescale mismatch
hypotheses.question: What happens when production outpaces scrutiny?
hypotheses.text: When AI accelerates rule production faster than institutions can scrutinize its consequences, unreviewed rules and errors may accumulate. Shared models may amplify correlated mistakes, weakening rather than strengthening institutional correction.
